name: Oral cysteine / NAC for pigment

lead: N-acetylcysteine is a medicine and supplement that supplies cysteine, a building block of glutathione. Some people take it in the hope of lightening pigment.
The sources reviewed contain no study of NAC or cysteine for skin pigment, and Wikipedia's article on the drug does not mention it.

paras: It raises cysteine availability and so can replenish glutathione; the link from glutathione to visible skin tone is the claim, not an established finding.
Oral use can cause nausea, vomiting, rash and fever. Oral bioavailability is only about 6 to 10 percent.

lead: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a prodrug of the amino acid L-cysteine, which is a precursor of the antioxidant glutathione. Some people in appearance and skin-lightening circles take oral NAC or cysteine in the belief that raising glutathione will lighten skin pigment.[1]

NAC is an established medicine for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and as a mucolytic, and it is sold as a dietary supplement. Wikipedia's article does not mention skin pigment or lightening, and no clinical study of oral cysteine or NAC for pigmentation was found among the sources reviewed.[1]

paras: The established uses are treating paracetamol overdose, where it helps restore glutathione to neutralize a toxic metabolite, and thinning mucus in chronic lung conditions. A 2013 Cochrane review found no evidence of benefit in cystic fibrosis. It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[1]

Because NAC supplies cysteine, it can replenish glutathione stores, and Wikipedia adds that its effects are not fully explained by glutathione alone, since it may also act through hydrogen sulfide production.[1] The idea behind the pigment claim is that glutathione status influences melanin production; the article does not describe such an effect.[1]
No studies found of oral cysteine or NAC for skin pigmentation or lightening.

Oral use has lower tolerability than intravenous use because of taste and odor, with nausea, vomiting, rash and fever reported. Intravenous use has caused rash, hives and itching, and about 3 to 6 percent of people have had a severe anaphylaxis-like reaction.[1]

lore.intro: Oral NAC and cysteine come up in skin-lightening discussions as glutathione boosters, though the sources reviewed contain no forum material.

claims.claim: Taking NAC or cysteine raises glutathione and lightens skin
